published_figures.source: Boeing D6-58325-6 rev E, 2023; FAA TCDS A16WE
published_figures.figure: Figure 3.3.11, page 3-20: FAR take-off runway length, CFM56-3B1 at 20,000 lb, standard day, sea level, no air-conditioning bleed, flaps 5, at 135,000 lb - about 8,400 ft, read from the chart.

FAR 25.121(b), the 737-300's certification basis (A16WE): with one engine out, the take-off flaps, the gear up and V2, a twin climbs at no less than 2.4%. No figure above that is published; 10% bounds a model gone wrong.
Level at 35,000 ft at full throttle, it must reach its cruise Mach, 0.74 (EUROCONTROL's Aircraft Performance Database; secondary), and its drag rise hold it within 0.03 of its Mmo, 0.82 (A16WE).
A16WE: maximum operating altitude 37,000 ft. As light as it flies, at full throttle, it still climbs there at 300 ft/min, the margin that makes an altitude a thrust-limited ceiling.

**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook stall speed to hold the model to. This is what the model itself does, flown by the same deceleration the published stall speeds are measured by, on 2026-09-23. What it asserts is that the model still does what it did, not that the aeroplane does it. Measured from entry speeds of 160, 200 and 240 knots it varies by 0.15 of a knot, so the number is the model's and not the entry's.

**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook rate of climb and no handbook climbing speed. Both are the model's own, taken on 2026-09-23. Sweeping 200 to 420 knots the best rate is 4666 ft/min at 320 knots; this is the lowest speed that still climbs within ninety-five per cent of it, which is the speed a climb is actually flown at. Taking the peak itself would have taught a climb faster than the aeroplane is operated.
